tagline: A Persian court official's own account of rebuilding Jerusalem's walls, renewing the covenant under the law of Moses, and fighting to keep a restored people faithful.
overview:
Nehemiah was a Jew serving as cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes I in the royal city of Susa. In 445 BC he hears that the walls of Jerusalem still lie broken and its gates burned, nearly a century after the first exiles came home. He prays, risks his position by asking the king for leave, and comes to Jerusalem as governor. Against mockery, threats, and plots from neighboring officials, he organizes the people to rebuild the whole circuit of the wall, and it is finished in fifty-two days (6:15).

The wall is only the first half of the book. Once the city is secure, Ezra reads the law of Moses to the assembled people (chapter 8), the people confess their sins in a long prayer that retells Israel's history (chapter 9), and they sign a binding agreement to keep the law (chapter 10). Nehemiah then repopulates the thinly settled city, and the wall is dedicated with two great choirs processing on top of it. The book ends with Nehemiah returning after an absence to find the people slipping back into the very failings they had promised to avoid, and dealing with them sharply.

Nehemiah is one of the most personal books of the Old Testament. Much of it is his own memoir, full of quick prayers, strong feelings, and honest self-defense. It shows a layman in government work who treats prayer and planning as partners, and it shows a community learning that walls, however necessary, cannot by themselves make a people faithful.
author:
Large parts of the book are written in the first person by Nehemiah himself (1:1 to 7:5, the dedication of the wall in 12:27-43, and most of chapter 13). This material is usually called the Nehemiah Memoir, and most scholars, whatever their other views, accept it as substantially his. Its style, with short prayers asking God to remember him (5:19, 13:14, 13:31), is distinctive. The rest of the book, including the list of returnees in chapter 7 (which repeats Ezra 2), the account of Ezra's reading of the law in chapters 8 to 10, and the lists of chapters 11 and 12, comes from other sources.

In the Hebrew tradition Ezra and Nehemiah were one book, and the same compiler shaped both. Jewish tradition in the Talmud credits Ezra with writing the book and Nehemiah with completing it. Modern scholars debate whether the compiler also wrote Chronicles; many now think Ezra-Nehemiah is a separate work, while others still see a close link. The book was later divided, and in some older Christian Bibles Nehemiah was called Second Esdras.
date:
The events are unusually well dated. Nehemiah receives the news in the month of Chislev in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes (1:1) and speaks to the king in Nisan of that year (2:1). With Artaxerxes I, who reigned 465-424 BC, this places Nehemiah's arrival in Jerusalem in 445 BC. He served as governor for twelve years, until the king's thirty-second year, 433 BC (5:14, 13:6), then returned to the king and came back to Jerusalem some time later. The Elephantine papyri, letters from a Jewish community in southern Egypt dated about 407 BC, mention the sons of Sanballat, governor of Samaria, and a high priest named Johanan in Jerusalem, which fits the setting of Nehemiah well.

The relative order of Ezra and Nehemiah is debated (see the introduction to Ezra), since Nehemiah 8 and 12 show them together. The book in its final form, with priestly lists running to Jaddua (12:11, 22), probably dates from around 400 BC or somewhat later.
setting:
Nehemiah lives at the heart of the Persian Empire. Susa, in what is now southwestern Iran, was one of the royal capitals, and a cupbearer served the king his wine and was expected to be utterly trustworthy, which gave him rare access to the king. Judah (Yehud) was a small province within the satrapy Beyond the River, west of the Euphrates. Jerusalem itself was thinly populated, and its walls had lain in ruins since the Babylonians broke them down in 587 or 586 BC. An earlier attempt to rebuild them had been stopped by royal order (Ezra 4:7-23).

The neighbors were powerful and wary. Sanballat the Horonite was governor of Samaria to the north. Tobiah, the Ammonite official, had influence east of the Jordan and ties by marriage to leading families in Jerusalem. Geshem the Arab probably represents the Arab kingdom of Qedar to the south; a silver bowl found at Tell el-Maskhuta in Egypt names a Qaynu son of Gashmu, king of Qedar, whom many identify as Geshem's son. Inside Judah, the people faced heavy taxes, debt, and poor harvests, and some were selling their children into servitude (chapter 5).
purpose: The book was written for the post-exilic community to show how God restored Jerusalem as a city and its people as a covenant community, and to call that community to lasting faithfulness. It holds up Nehemiah as an example of prayerful, courageous leadership, and it presents the reading of the law and the renewal of the covenant as the true center of the restoration. Its unresolved ending is part of its purpose: it warns that promises made in a great assembly must be kept in ordinary weeks, in the matters of the Sabbath, the temple's upkeep, and marriage.
story: Nehemiah continues the story told in Ezra. The first exiles returned under Cyrus in 538 BC and finished the temple in 515 BC; Ezra came with a second group in 458 BC (on the traditional dating). About thirteen years later Nehemiah arrives to rebuild the city walls. His book is the last historical narrative of the Old Testament, and the prophet Malachi, who confronts many of the same problems (careless priests, neglected tithes, broken marriages), probably spoke in the same general period. After Nehemiah the Old Testament story falls silent until the New Testament opens in a Jerusalem ruled by Rome, whose temple and walls descend, through later rebuilding, from the work of these years.
christ: Nehemiah shows a restored city that is still waiting. The walls are rebuilt, the law is read, and the covenant is renewed, yet in the great prayer of chapter 9 the people say that they are slaves in their own land, with foreign kings ruling over them. The book ends with Nehemiah asking God to remember him, not with a kingdom established. The Old Testament's longing for a true restoration, a new covenant written on the heart and a king who would build God's house forever, remains open. The New Testament finds that longing met in Jesus, who weeps over Jerusalem, cleanses its temple, and brings a covenant in which the law is written on hearts. The links here are mostly thematic: Nehemiah's intercession for his people, his costly leaving of the palace for a ruined city, and his zeal for God's house are patterns the Gospels fill with greater meaning, not predictions the book makes.
reading: Read Nehemiah as a memoir set inside a larger historical book. Listen for Nehemiah's voice: his quick prayers in the middle of action (2:4), his lament, his anger, and his repeated appeals to God to remember him. Don't skip the lists of builders, returnees, and signers, which record the names of ordinary people who did the work. Notice how the book turns at chapter 8 from building the city to building the people, and that the high point is not the wall's completion but the reading of the law. Finally, read the harsh measures of chapter 13 with care. The book presents Nehemiah as sincere and largely in the right, but it also lets the reader see a reform that must be enforced again and again, which is part of its message.

structure.title: Nehemiah's burden and commission
structure.summary: In Susa Nehemiah hears of Jerusalem's ruin, prays, asks Artaxerxes for leave, and arrives in Jerusalem, where he inspects the walls by night and calls the people to build.

structure.title: The wall rebuilt against opposition
structure.summary: Families and groups rebuild the wall section by section, while Nehemiah faces mockery, threats of attack, economic injustice among the Jews themselves, and plots against his life. The wall is finished in fifty-two days, and Nehemiah turns to the city's population, using the list of the first returnees.

structure.title: The law read and the covenant renewed
structure.summary: Ezra reads the law to the assembled people, who celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles, confess their sins in a great prayer, and sign a binding agreement to keep God's commands.

structure.title: A city peopled and a wall dedicated
structure.summary: One in ten of the people move into Jerusalem, the lists of priests and Levites are recorded, and the wall is dedicated with processions and great joy.

structure.title: Nehemiah's final reforms
structure.summary: Returning after an absence, Nehemiah expels Tobiah from a temple chamber, restores support for the Levites, enforces the Sabbath, and confronts marriages outside the covenant.

themes.title: Prayer and action together
themes.body: Nehemiah prays at length when he hears the news (chapter 1), prays in a single breath before answering the king (2:4), and sets guards while praying against attack. The book never sets prayer against planning. It treats careful work, risk, and organization as ways of trusting God.

themes.title: The people of God rebuilt
themes.body: The wall is rebuilt by dozens of families, guilds, and towns, each at its own section, and the book records their names. Restoration is a shared work. The same book insists that a people is rebuilt not only by stones but by hearing God's word, confessing sin, and binding themselves to obey.

themes.title: Opposition from without and within
themes.body: Enemies mock, threaten, and scheme, and some of the danger comes from inside: nobles who exploit the poor, prophets hired to frighten Nehemiah, and a priest who gave Tobiah a room in the temple. The book is honest that the community's worst threats are sometimes its own members.

themes.title: Justice for the poor
themes.body: In chapter 5 Nehemiah stops the building to confront Jews who were charging interest to their own brothers and taking their fields and children for debts. He cancels the debts and refuses the governor's food allowance. For this book, a rebuilt city with an unjust economy is not a restored city.

themes.title: Covenant faithfulness in ordinary life
themes.body: The covenant of chapter 10 is concrete: marriage, the Sabbath, the temple tax, firstfruits, and tithes. Chapter 13 shows those very commitments failing. Faithfulness, in Nehemiah, is measured in markets, storerooms, and households, and it has to be renewed.

keyChapters.why: Nehemiah's prayer of confession, grounded in God's covenant promises to Moses, shows how the book's action begins in intercession.
Nehemiah risks his post before the king, receives leave to rebuild, and calls the people of Jerusalem to begin the work.
Nehemiah halts the project to confront the exploitation of poor Jews by their own nobles, showing that justice belongs to rebuilding.
Ezra reads the law to the whole people, the Levites explain it, and the people's weeping turns to joy in the Feast of Tabernacles.
A great prayer retells Israel's history as a story of God's faithfulness and the people's rebellion, and admits they are still slaves in their own land.
The book ends not in triumph but with renewed failure and renewed reform, and with Nehemiah asking God to remember him.

parts.body:
Nehemiah is the sixteenth book of the Bible. It has thirteen chapters, and it tells how a Jewish official at the Persian court came to Jerusalem in 445 BC, rebuilt the city's broken walls in fifty-two days, and then worked to rebuild the people who lived inside them.

The book has two halves. In chapters 1 to 7, Nehemiah hears that Jerusalem's wall is broken down, prays, asks the king for leave, and leads the people to rebuild the wall section by section against mockery, threats and plots. In chapters 8 to 13 the story turns from stones to Scripture. Ezra reads the law to the people, they confess their sins, they sign a pledge to keep God's commands, the city is filled with people, and the wall is dedicated with two great choirs singing on top of it. Then Nehemiah goes away for a time, comes back, and finds the people breaking the very promises they had made.

Some of its scenes stay with readers: a cupbearer who prays silently between the king's question and his own answer (2:4); builders who ‘worked with one hand and held a weapon with the other’ (4:17); a crowd standing from dawn to noon to hear the law read; and the day when ‘the joy of Jerusalem was heard from afar’ (12:43).

Much of the book is Nehemiah's own account, written in the first person, full of quick prayers, strong feelings and honest self-defense. It shows a layman in government work who treats prayer and planning as partners. And it ends without a triumph. Its last words are a prayer: ‘Remember me, O my God, with favor’ (13:31). Walls, the book admits, cannot by themselves make a people faithful.

parts.h: Where it sits in the story
parts.body:
Nehemiah carries on the story told in Ezra. The first exiles came home under Cyrus in 538 BC and finished the temple in 515 BC. Ezra came with a second group in 458 BC, on the traditional dating. About thirteen years later Nehemiah arrives to rebuild the city's walls, nearly a century after the first return.

In the Hebrew Bible, Ezra and Nehemiah are one book, among the Writings. Christian Bibles divide them and place Nehemiah among the books of history, after Ezra and before Esther. In some older Christian Bibles, Nehemiah was called Second Esdras.

The book is the last historical narrative of the Old Testament. The prophet Malachi, who confronts many of the same problems, careless priests, neglected tithes and broken marriages, probably spoke in the same general period. After Nehemiah the Old Testament's story falls silent until the New Testament opens, some four centuries later, in a Jerusalem ruled by Rome, whose temple and walls descend, through later rebuilding, from the work of these years.

Large parts of the book are written in the first person by Nehemiah himself: from 1:1 to 7:5, the dedication of the wall in 12:27-43, and most of chapter 13. Scholars call this the Nehemiah Memoir, and most of them, whatever their other views, accept it as substantially his. Its voice is unmistakable, especially in its short prayers asking God to remember him (5:19; 13:14, 31).

The rest of the book comes from other sources: the list of the first returnees in chapter 7, which repeats Ezra 2; the account of Ezra's reading of the law and the people's response in chapters 8 to 10; and the lists of chapters 11 and 12.

In the Hebrew tradition, Ezra and Nehemiah were one book, shaped by the same compiler. Jewish tradition in the Talmud credits Ezra with writing it and Nehemiah with completing it. Modern scholars debate whether the compiler also wrote Chronicles; many now think Ezra and Nehemiah form a separate work, while others still see a close link.

The book in its final form, with priestly lists that run to Jaddua (12:11, 22), probably dates from around 400 BC or somewhat later. The Bible does not claim that Nehemiah wrote every line of the book that bears his name, and ancient records were often brought up to date by later scribes. On every view, the memoir at its heart is his.

The events are unusually well dated. Nehemiah hears the news ‘In the month of Chislev, in the twentieth year’ (1:1), and he speaks to the king in the month of Nisan ‘in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes’ (2:1). The king is Artaxerxes I, who reigned from 465 to 424 BC, so Nehemiah came to Jerusalem in 445 BC.

There is a small puzzle. Nisan is the first month of the usual year, so it would come before Chislev, not after. Scholars explain this in different ways: Nehemiah may have counted the king's years from the anniversary of his accession, or from an autumn new year, or the text of 1:1 may first have read the nineteenth year. The difference does not change the story.

The wall was finished on the twenty-fifth of Elul (6:15), in the late summer or early autumn of 445 BC. Nehemiah served as governor for twelve years, until the king's thirty-second year, 433 BC (5:14). Then he went back to the king, and he returned to Jerusalem some time later (13:6). Some date his second term to around 430 BC; the book does not say how long he was away.

The relative order of Ezra and Nehemiah is debated, since Nehemiah 8 and 12 show them together. Most readers keep the traditional order, with Ezra arriving in 458 BC and Nehemiah in 445 BC. Some scholars date Ezra's arrival after Nehemiah's, to 398 BC, and regard their joint appearances as the work of a later editor. Careful readers hold each view, and these notes take no side.

parts.h: Susa, the cupbearer, and three rivals
parts.body:
Nehemiah lives at the heart of the Persian empire. Susa, in what is now southwestern Iran, was one of its royal capitals, where the kings often spent the winter, and archaeologists have dug up the great palace that Darius I built there. The book of Esther is set in the same city.

Nehemiah is the king's cupbearer (1:11). A cupbearer served the king his wine and often tasted it first to guard against poison. The post needed complete trust, and it gave daily access to the king. That access is why Nehemiah could ask the king for anything at all.

Judah was a small province within the Persian region west of the Euphrates. Jerusalem was thinly settled, and its walls had lain in ruins since the Babylonians broke them down in 587 or 586 BC. An earlier attempt to rebuild them had been stopped by royal order (Ezra 4:7-23).

The neighbors were powerful and wary. Sanballat the Horonite was governor of Samaria to the north. A letter of 407 BC from the Jewish community at Elephantine in Egypt names the sons of Sanballat, governor of Samaria, which fits him well. Tobiah, the Ammonite official, had influence east of the Jordan and ties by marriage to leading families in Jerusalem. Papyri from about 259 BC name a local magnate called Tobias, probably of the same family. Geshem the Arab probably stands for the Arab kingdom of Qedar to the south. A silver bowl found at Tell el-Maskhuta in Egypt names a Qaynu son of Gashmu, king of Qedar, whom many identify as Geshem's son. A walled Jerusalem threatened the influence all three held over Judah.

The book turns at chapter 8. Chapters 1 to 7 are about building the city: the news and the prayer (1), the king's leave and the night inspection (2), the builders (3), the opposition and the armed workers (4), the poor and the nobles (5), the plots and the finished wall (6), and the list of those who first came home (7). Chapters 8 to 13 are about building the people: the law read (8), the great prayer of confession (9), the pledge (10), the city filled (11), the wall dedicated (12), and the last reforms (13).

The high point of the book is not the finished wall but the reading of the law. And the ending is deliberately unresolved. The people break the promises of chapter 10, Nehemiah confronts them again, and the book closes with a tired leader asking God to remember him.

The lists matter. Chapter 3 names the people who built each section of the wall; chapter 7 copies out the register of those who first came home; chapters 10 to 12 name those who signed the pledge, those who lived in the city, and the priests and Levites. The book records the names of ordinary people who did the work.

And watch for Nehemiah's short prayers, breaking into the story in the middle of action: ‘Hear us, O God, for we are despised’ (4:4); ‘But now, my God, strengthen my hands’ (6:9); ‘Remember me favorably, O my God, for all that I have done for this people’ (5:19). They are the memoir's signature.

parts.h: Prayer, a king, and a night ride
parts.body:
The book begins with grief. In Susa, Nehemiah's brother Hanani brings word that the people in Judah are ‘in great trouble and disgrace. The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates are burned with fire’ (1:3). Nehemiah sits down and weeps, mourns for days, fasts and prays.

His prayer is built from Scripture. It praises ‘the great and awesome God who keeps His covenant of loving devotion’ (1:5), confesses Israel's sins, his own family's among them, and reminds God of his promise through Moses to gather a scattered people who turn back to him. Then it asks for something specific: success before ‘this man’ (1:11), the king.

Four months later, Nehemiah serves the king wine with a sad face. In the Persian court, sorrow in the king's presence could be dangerous, and he is afraid. The king asks, “What is your request?” (2:4). ‘So I prayed to the God of heaven’ (2:4), Nehemiah writes, and then he answers. After months of prayer, a quick silent prayer is enough. He asks to be sent to rebuild ‘the city where my fathers are buried’ (2:5), and the king grants it, with letters for the governors, timber from the king's forest, and an escort of officers and cavalry.

In Jerusalem Nehemiah tells no one his plans at first. He rides out by night to inspect the broken walls, and where rubble blocks the way, his animal cannot pass. Then he calls the leaders: ‘Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, so that we will no longer be a disgrace’ (2:17). And they answer, ‘Let us start rebuilding’ (2:18).

The book never sets prayer against planning. Nehemiah prays at length, prays in a single breath, and plans with care, and he sees all of it under ‘the gracious hand of my God’ (2:8).

parts.h: The wall: builders, enemies and fifty-two days
parts.body:
Chapter 3 goes around the wall section by section, gate by gate, and names who built each part. Priests built near the temple. Goldsmiths, perfumers and merchants took sections. Men came from Jericho, Gibeon, Tekoa and other towns. Many repaired the wall in front of their own houses. One ruler worked ‘with the help of his daughters’ (3:12). Only the nobles of Tekoa are singled out for refusing to put their shoulders to the work.

The opposition grows as the wall rises. First comes mockery. Sanballat asks whether the Jews can ‘bring these burnt stones back to life from the mounds of rubble’ (4:2), and Tobiah jokes that a fox could knock their wall down. Then comes a plot to attack. Nehemiah's answer is the book in a sentence: ‘So we prayed to our God and posted a guard against them day and night’ (4:9). Half the men build and half stand guard, and the laborers work with one hand and hold a weapon with the other.

When the attack fails, the plots turn on Nehemiah himself. His enemies invite him four times to a meeting far from Jerusalem, where they mean to harm him. They send an open letter accusing him of planning a revolt. They hire a prophet to frighten him into hiding in the temple, where a layman had no right to go. Nehemiah sees through each one: “I am doing a great work and cannot come down” (6:3).

‘So the wall was completed in fifty-two days, on the twenty-fifth of Elul’ (6:15). Even the surrounding nations, the book says, ‘realized that this task had been accomplished by our God’ (6:16).

Fifty-two days is fast. Much of the old foundation could be used again, the work was divided among many teams, and the circuit Nehemiah rebuilt was smaller than the city before the exile. Most scholars think his Jerusalem covered only the temple mount and the narrow ridge of the old City of David.

In the middle of the building, Nehemiah stops to deal with a threat from inside. Ordinary families cry out that famine, the king's tax and debt have forced them to mortgage their fields and to sell their children into slavery to wealthier Jews. ‘Some of our daughters are already enslaved, but we are powerless to redeem them because our fields and vineyards belong to others’ (5:5).

The law of Moses allowed lending, but it forbade charging interest to a poor fellow Israelite. It allowed a poor man to sell his labor to pay a debt, but it required that he be treated as a hired worker and set free in the year of release. Those protections had broken down.

Nehemiah is very angry. He calls a public assembly and confronts the nobles and officials: “What you are doing is not right. Shouldn’t you walk in the fear of our God to avoid the reproach of our foreign enemies?” (5:9). They agree to stop charging interest and to give back the fields, vineyards and houses they have taken, and Nehemiah makes them swear to it, shaking out the fold of his robe as a sign of what would happen to anyone who broke the oath.

Then he describes his own twelve years as governor. The governors before him had laid heavy burdens on the people. He refused the food allowance he was entitled to, and fed many at his own table at his own cost, ‘because of my fear of God’ (5:15). For this book, a rebuilt city with an unjust economy is not a restored city.

parts.h: The law read, a people confessing, a pledge signed
parts.body:
When the wall is finished, the story turns from stones to Scripture. In the seventh month the people gather in the square before the Water Gate and ask Ezra the scribe to bring out the Book of the Law of Moses. ‘So Ezra read it aloud from daybreak until noon’ (8:3), standing on a wooden platform, while the people stood. The Levites moved among them: ‘explaining it and giving insight, so that the people could understand what was being read’ (8:8).

The people weep as they hear it. But Nehemiah, Ezra and the Levites tell them that the day is holy, and that they should feast and send portions to those who have nothing: “Do not grieve, for the joy of the LORD is your strength” (8:10). Then they find in the law the command to live in booths at the Feast of Tabernacles, and they keep it with a joy not seen ‘From the days of Joshua son of Nun until that day’ (8:17).

Later in the month comes the mourning they had held back. The people fast, confess their sins, and the Levites lead one of the longest prayers in the Bible, retelling Israel's story from creation to the exile. It praises a God who is ‘gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and rich in loving devotion’ (9:17), and it admits a long history of stiff necks. It ends with the people still subjects of a foreign king: ‘So here we are today as slaves in the land You gave our fathers to enjoy its fruit and goodness’ (9:36).

Then they put their promises in writing. Nehemiah, the priests, the Levites and the leaders seal a binding pledge, and the rest of the people swear ‘to follow the Law of God given through His servant Moses’ (10:29). They promise not to intermarry with the peoples around them, not to buy on the Sabbath, to keep the seventh year, and to support the house of God. The pledge ends, ‘Thus we will not neglect the house of our God’ (10:39).

parts.h: A city filled, and a wall dedicated
parts.body:
A wall does not make a city. ‘Now the city was large and spacious, but there were few people in it, and the houses had not yet been rebuilt’ (7:4). So the leaders settle in Jerusalem, and the rest of the people cast lots to bring one family in ten to live in the holy city (11:1). Many preferred to live where their land was, since farming was their living, and moving into the city meant giving up property and security. ‘And the people blessed all the men who volunteered to live in Jerusalem’ (11:2).

Then the wall is dedicated. The Levites and singers are gathered from the villages around the city. The priests purify themselves, then the people, the gates and the wall. Two great choirs giving thanks climb onto the wall and walk around it in opposite directions, one with Ezra and one with Nehemiah, until they meet at the house of God. ‘On that day they offered great sacrifices, rejoicing because God had given them great joy. The women and children also rejoiced, so that the joy of Jerusalem was heard from afar’ (12:43).

The book also sees to the plain work behind the joy. Officials are appointed over the storerooms, so that the priests, Levites, singers and gatekeepers receive the portions the law gave them.

parts.h: Broken promises, and Nehemiah's last reforms
parts.body:
The book could have ended with the joy of chapter 12. Instead it ends with an honest look at how quickly a community can drift.

Nehemiah had gone back to the king in the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes, 433 BC (13:6). When he returns, he finds nearly every promise of chapter 10 broken. A priest named Eliashib has given Tobiah, the old opponent, a room in the temple's storehouse. The Levites have not been given their portions, and they have gone back to their fields. People are working and trading in Jerusalem on the Sabbath, and men of Tyre are selling fish there. And men of Judah have married women from Ashdod, Ammon and Moab, and half their children cannot speak the language of Judah. Even a grandson of the high priest has married Sanballat's daughter.

Nehemiah acts. He throws Tobiah's belongings out of the temple room, restores the tithes and the Levites, shuts the city gates before the Sabbath, and confronts the men who married foreign women. He tells of it himself, without softening: ‘I rebuked them and called down curses on them. I beat some of these men and pulled out their hair’ (13:25). He makes them swear not to give their children in marriage to the peoples around them, and he points to Solomon, who was ‘loved by his God’ (13:26) and was still drawn into sin.

The text reports what Nehemiah did and does not comment on it, and readers weigh it in two ways. Some see the harsh but lawful discipline of a governor facing a threat to the community's survival, in a culture where public shaming was a normal punishment. Others see a zealous leader whose methods went beyond what was right, and they notice that the book ends with Nehemiah asking for mercy rather than claiming to be in the right. Either way, a story describes what happened without by that fact recommending it. Nothing in this chapter gives anyone today a warrant to strike or harm anyone, at home, in a church or anywhere else.

The question of the marriages is the same one Ezra faced, and the notes on Ezra 9 and 10 set out how readers weigh it. The concern in Nehemiah is faithfulness to God; Ruth the Moabite, who took Israel's God as her own, is the example the Bible itself keeps. And the book ends where a reader least expects: ‘Remember me, O my God, with favor’ (13:31).

parts.h: How the New Testament reads Nehemiah
parts.body:
The New Testament says little about Nehemiah, and it is wise to keep to the lines it does draw.

The Jerusalem of the Gospels, with its walls and its temple, descends through later rebuilding from the work of these years. John names one of Nehemiah's gates: ‘Now there is in Jerusalem near the Sheep Gate a pool with five covered colonnades’ (John 5:2).

The practices of this book run on into the New Testament world. The people's pledge to give ‘a third of a shekel yearly for the service of the house of our God’ (10:32) stands behind the temple tax that collectors ask Peter about (Matthew 17:24). The public reading of the law, explained so that people could understand, is what Paul asks Timothy to keep at: ‘devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, and to teaching’ (1 Timothy 4:13). And when Paul shakes out his garments in Corinth (Acts 18:6), he makes the same kind of sign Nehemiah made with the fold of his robe (5:13).

Some Christians have read Nehemiah, who left a palace for a ruined city and interceded for his people, as a picture of Christ. The book's own introduction calls such links thematic, and the New Testament does not draw that line; these notes do not draw it either. Nothing in the book, or in the New Testament's use of it, is a reason to blame or look down on the Jewish people, or on the peoples whose leaders opposed the wall.

A few habits will help a new reader.

Read it as a memoir inside a larger book. Listen for Nehemiah's voice: his quick prayers in the middle of action (2:4), his grief, his anger, and his repeated asking God to remember him.

Do not skip the lists of builders, returnees and signers. They record the names of ordinary people who did the work.

Notice the turn at chapter 8. The high point of the book is not the finished wall but the reading of the law, and the joy of a people who understood it.

Read chapter 5 slowly. It shows that the poor matter to God as much as the walls do.

Read chapter 13 with care. The book presents Nehemiah as sincere and largely in the right, but it also lets the reader see a reform that has to be enforced again and again, and harsh acts told without approval. That is part of its message: promises made in a great assembly have to be kept in ordinary weeks.

And read Malachi beside the last chapters. The same careless priests, neglected tithes and broken marriages appear in both.

hard.line: Chislev before Nisan in the same twentieth year: how the king's years were counted.
Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem: who they were, and why a walled Jerusalem threatened them.
The builders of the wall, and the nobles of Tekoa who would not put their shoulders to the work.
Nehemiah prays that his enemies' sin not be blotted out: a cry for justice handed to God.
Building with one hand and holding a weapon with the other: armed only for defense.
Families forced to sell their children into slavery to their own people, and why the law allowed debt service at all.
A hired prophet, and how Nehemiah knew that God had not sent him.
The list of the first returnees again: its figures differ from Ezra 2 and fall short of the total.
‘Explaining it and giving insight’: reading clearly, or translating into Aramaic?
No such Feast of Tabernacles since Joshua's day, though the Bible records earlier ones.
The ordinances ‘by which a man will live if he practices them’, and how Paul reads the same words.
A pledge that differs in places from the law of Moses: a third of a shekel, wood by lot, no Sabbath trade.
Lists that run to Jaddua and a later Darius: who wrote them, and when.
The law excluding Ammonites and Moabites read aloud, and Ruth the Moabite in David's line.
Nehemiah beats men and pulls out their hair: told without comment, and no warrant for harming anyone today.
A book that ends not in triumph but with a prayer to be remembered.

words.line: The royal servant who poured the king's wine and tasted it first. The post needed complete trust and gave daily access to the king (1:11).
The Hebrew chesed: God's faithful covenant love. Nehemiah's first prayer begins with the God ‘who keeps His covenant of loving devotion’ (1:5).
The Hebrew zakar: to bring to mind in a way that leads to action. Nehemiah asks God to remember his word (1:8), to remember Nehemiah (5:19; 13:31), and to remember his enemies (6:14).
The Hebrew cherpah, reproach. A ruined city shamed its people and the God whose name it bore. The wall was rebuilt so that the people would be a disgrace no longer (2:17).
The Hebrew chazaq, to be strong. The people strengthen their hands for the work (2:18), and the same verb is the word for repairing the wall, again and again in chapter 3.
The Hebrew pardes, a Persian word for an enclosed park, here the king's forest (2:8). Its Greek form later gave English the word paradise.
The Hebrew melakhah, used for the rebuilding throughout. The enemies want to stop the work, and the people keep returning to it (4:6; 6:3).
The Hebrew tseaqah, the cry of the oppressed that God hears, as Israel cried out in Egypt. The poor raise it in 5:1.
Reverent awe that shapes behavior. Nehemiah gives it as the reason the nobles should stop exploiting the poor (5:9) and the reason he refused his allowance (5:15).
The Hebrew bin. It runs through chapter 8: those who could understand, the Levites helping them understand, and the people rejoicing because they understood (8:2, 8, 12).
The Hebrew sukkot, shelters of branches. Israel lived in them at the Feast of Tabernacles to remember the wilderness years (8:14-17).
The Hebrew rachamim, related to the word for womb. The great prayer gives it as the reason Israel still exists: in God's great compassion he did not forsake them (9:19, 27, 28, 31).
The Hebrew amanah, a firm commitment, from the root of amen. The people put their pledge in writing and seal it (9:38).
The Hebrew chanukkah, the setting apart of the finished wall for God (12:27). The same word later named the feast of Hanukkah.
The seventh day of rest, named ten times in chapter 13. Nehemiah shuts the gates to keep it holy (13:19-22).

timeline.what: Cyrus takes Babylon, and the next year the first exiles go home (Ezra 1).
The second temple is finished in Darius's sixth year (Ezra 6:15).
Artaxerxes I reigns over Persia. His officials have the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls stopped (Ezra 4:7-23).
Ezra comes to Jerusalem with a second group of exiles (Ezra 7:7-9).
In the month of Chislev, in Susa, Nehemiah hears that Jerusalem's wall is broken down (1:1-3).
In Nisan of the king's twentieth year, Nehemiah asks Artaxerxes for leave to rebuild (2:1-8).
The wall is finished in fifty-two days, on the twenty-fifth of Elul (6:15).

timeline.when: Autumn 445 BC, if the chapters follow in order
timeline.what: Ezra reads the law, the Feast of Tabernacles is kept, the people confess, and the pledge is sealed (chapters 8 to 10).
Nehemiah's first term as governor of Judah, from the twentieth to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes (5:14).
Nehemiah goes back to the king (13:6).

timeline.when: Some time later, about 430 BC on one reckoning
timeline.what: Nehemiah returns to Jerusalem and finds the pledges broken (13:6-31). The book does not say how long he was away.
Darius II reigns, possibly the ‘Darius the Persian’ of 12:22, though some think of Darius III.
The Jews at Elephantine in Egypt write to the governor of Judah, naming the sons of Sanballat and the high priest Johanan.
Some scholars place Ezra's arrival here, after Nehemiah.
Ezra and Nehemiah, one book, reach their final form; the priestly lists run to Jaddua (12:11, 22).
Papyri from the archive of Zenon name a local magnate, Tobias, probably of the family of Nehemiah's opponent Tobiah.
Kathleen Kenyon finds collapsed terraces on the eastern slope of the City of David, and Nahman Avigad uncovers a massive wall he names the Broad Wall after 3:8.

map.title: Jerusalem and the land around it in Nehemiah's day

places.name: Jerusalem
places.line: The city whose wall Nehemiah rebuilt in fifty-two days (6:15) and dedicated with two choirs singing on top of it (12:27-43).

places.name: Bethlehem
places.line: ‘The men of Bethlehem and Netophah’ are on the list of those who first came home (7:26).

places.name: Bethel
places.line: Its men are on the list of the first return (7:32), and Benjamin's people lived there in Nehemiah's day (11:31).

places.name: Jericho
places.line: ‘The men of Jericho built next to Eliashib’ the high priest, near the Sheep Gate (3:2).

places.name: Lod
places.line: The town later called Lydda. Its people were among the first to come home (7:37), and Benjamin's people lived there (11:35). The plain of Ono, where Nehemiah's enemies tried to lure him (6:2), lay nearby.

places.name: Hebron
places.line: Called by its old name, Kiriath-arba. Some of the people of Judah lived there and in its villages (11:25).

places.name: Beersheba
places.line: The people of Judah ‘settled from Beersheba all the way to the Valley of Hinnom’ (11:30).

places.name: Ashdod
places.line: The old Philistine city on the coast. Its people joined the plot against the wall (4:7), and some men of Judah married women from there (13:23-24).

places.name: Samaria
places.line: The province to the north, governed by Sanballat. He mocked the builders before ‘the army of Samaria’ (4:2). Drawn roughly.

places.name: Tyre
places.line: The Phoenician trading city. Its men sold fish and goods in Jerusalem on the Sabbath (13:16).

teaching.mapNote: Only ten places are drawn, each placed elsewhere on this site; Samaria roughly, as a region, Lod at the point used for Lydda, and Hebron under its later name. Susa lies far to the east and is not placed in this site's records; Ono, Gibeon, Mizpah, Tekoa, Beth-horon and the lands of Ammon and Qedar are left off too. No borders are drawn. The map makes no claim about any border today.
